animus/ANIMUS---BASAIRA-Reflections.title: ANIMUS - BASAIRA Reflections
animus/ANIMUS---BASAIRA-Reflections.content:
ANIMUS Methods
Baseline depth questionnaire
BFI self-evaluation

Evaluation so far
Recently, I managed to experiment with many different formats of psychological evaluation. I took an interest in leveraging LLMs (namely Opus 4.5 due it’s systematic approach and chat wide context mapping) to interpret my BFI scores, provide me with a journaling framework which would extract higher-dimensionality insights and then leveraging those responses in new LLM instances for separate BFI scoring.
The results showed that the contextually derived responses (journal questionnaire)  contained richer data which LLMs were able to leverage in their BFI scoring to provide more accurate scores (according to my interpretation) and crucially, be able to give the broader project (BASAIRA) directional queues which made more sense for my psychological profile - i.e. next steps and directions which are aligned with my long-term goals and philosophies. The additional layered insights which are embedded into the journal data provides richer insights which give deeper context for direction.
Thoughts and next steps
Considering the results and the promise in the ability of the smartest models to interpret ‘psycho-linguistic’ data such as journal entries, I would like to continue with my original plan of building a psycho-platform for which the rest of the BASAIRA learning framework could sit - as well as directional context on how best to design it.
Another remark I made was the difference in scoring styles and slight differences in verbiage and suggestions between models. I have not added structured frameworks for the models to follow in the form of skills or tools. I also left the temperature to 1 (in the gemini models where I could control it in the google-ai-studio interface). There were distinct traits and pattens in specific models, as well as model families. It is important to establish understandings of both model behaviours as well as desired model behaviours when interpreting qualitative data which becomes a foundation for decision making.
Analysing model psychology through similar (ANIMUS) frameworks also interests me and could provide novel insight.
How this affects and directs the BASAIRA project
The Basaira ethos and intentionality includes attempting to create a self-circulating learning system.
The ways in which I have been implementing ‘Basaira-like’ learning practices is as follows : I’ve been journaling, writing and documenting areas of my life and my projects as and when they progress and/or I discover new ideas. I tend to structure my workflow, projects and career generally - in a broad, unstructured, directionally-guided format in order to suit my observed learning patterns and corresponding states. Viewing myself as the primary driving system and orienting my external inputs and practises with the long-term goals in mind has also been critical. For example, retaining autonomy over the quality, type and format of content I ingest through eliminating algorithmic content suppliers such as Instagram reels and the YouTube homepage. This practice has allowed me to control the content I ingest and hence have more directional control over the thoughts I have and keep my mind focussed within the domains of interest to me. This has also meant that I’m having to provide myself with ‘balance’. Prioritising exercise, creative outputs and socialising has been crucial to prevent burn-out states. There also exists other key factors such as diet and supplements which are important, but I will not be visiting these concepts in depth in this article.

I want to expand on the functionality available to the interface layer of writing and spoken words, and conversation. From my experience, deepening understanding of a concept or area of exploration through written mediums such as ‘journal-like’ reflection or structured, intentional conversation has been very beneficial. I’ve been able to visualise and manipulate new learnings such that I strengthen the dimensionality of the new information in my mind.
LLMs have a few differentiating functionalities which make them a novel and new technology. One of these traits is their ability to understand semantic data, information which can only be ‘read from between the lines’. Previously, search engines like Google would encode semantic value through associative language, keywords, phrases etc. which link concepts through numerically prevalent means (if a word is frequently associated with a topic, internal algorithms would form links between the two). The advent of attention mechanisms and the Transformer architecture (the architecture of LLMs) has allowed semantic understanding to be encoded into the weights of the models (LLMs) themselves. All this to say that they can actually understand shit.
Most people intuitively pick up on this and smart users consciously architect the context window (the ‘chat’ - the sequence of messages between user and model (+ files etc.)). There is much research, deliberation and interest in optimising LLM performance by augmenting and manipulating the context from which the models generate their outputs. RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) and (hybrid) in-context based methods like Claude skills and MCP (Model Context Protocol) have come to be to boost the scope and depth of functionality of LLM agents in ‘real-world applications’. One of the most exciting and successful instances of intelligent use of context (and tools) are coding agents like CLI-based agents (i.e. Claude code), where the objective (‘design / build X according to Y spec’) is achieved through the agent’s navigation of what is available to it - navigating and adding data to it’s context, leveraging tools etc.
In order to attempt to build a system which enriches and supports learning experiences for user’s (through effective leverage of LLM agents), it is first important to understand user’s specific learning methods and general psychological patterns. The most effective method of increasing meaningful productive output for people is usually through implementing healthier habits and patterns - not a specific tool.
ANIMUS aims to create baseline and evolving user (psychological / habitual) profiles which can be used to direct model outputs and direct learning systems. Understanding how the user operates, what internal conflicts and ruminations they are currently having, as well as patterns which present themselves over time, can greatly improve the efficacy of a truly adaptive learning system.

Key challenges / obstacles in this approach
Psychological data encoding
Encoding psychological data is difficult in-of-in itself. The standard framework is the Big Five Index (ANIMUS leverages BFI2 - with further trait breakdowns) which scores the user across 5 broad traits (0-100) : Openness, Consensuses, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. See ANIMUS Methods for further project related breakdown of this framework and the OCEAN paper for the original paper detailing the framework.
So far, I’ve taken a version of the widely accepted BFI questionnaire, which asks the user to score themselves on various questions about themselves from Highly Disagree to Highly Agree, and I’ve also designed and utilised open-journaling questionnaires + LLM scoring to give BFI scores. See BFI self-evaluation for further insights into my baseline (BFI questionnaire) and ‘ANIMUS_v1’ (Agent) methods and scores.
In both methods, the original data: psychological profile, habits, thoughts, patterns, subconscious tendencies, goes through a self-evaluated rubric and is compressed to numerical values. The main value in ANIMUS, in leveraging open-ended reflective questioning is to retain and highlight the data-points which indicate those scores. These data-points are things such as habits, self-observed patterns and tendencies, ties of current personality to childhood events, all of which can be leveraged to predict future-behaviours.
Whilst filling out the open-ended evaluative questionnaire Baseline depth questionnaire, I naturally expressed evidence and/or explanation for my answers. For example :


What topics or skills have you learned fastest? What made those different?

I learn and understand topics much better and faster than skills as a whole. I can injest and understand, deeply-understand nuanced areas of research and abstact concepts very quickly. When it comes to skills, I find it difficult to stay disciplined with the inputs sometimes and such make progress slower. There is sometimes a frustration associated with the lack of pace towards the desired level of profficiency. The gap between now and the future me appears ‘too-long’.

The question above asks for a somewhat objective data-point with relation to how I’ve learning in the past. Answering the question in a conversational tone with a low (ideally zero) filter results in a natural disclosing of explanations for certain behaviours. The section of answer above provides evidence to inform multiple facets of BFI indicators. From the question alone, if it were posed on a scale basis (as in the traditional BFI questionnaire), and phrased as such ‘I learn skills faster than topics. - Highly Disagree ←> Highly Agree, the question would likely correlate to my Openness to experience in some form of numerical weighting (in conjunction with other answer scores). The additional context I naturally provide : ‘There is sometimes a frustration associated with the lack of pace..’ gives contextual evidence which can also be used to score Neurotiscm (Negative Emotionality).
The broader interpretation of questionnaire data in the above format gives LLM agents more practical evidence for scoring. Removing the scoring altogether and encoding or adding this data to an agent’s context with a prompt related to aiding the user’s learning would likely increase the results of the assisted ‘learning session’.
Context Augmentation (/Limits)
Thousands of Tokens in the form of journal-like questionnaires cannot be provided for every query or ‘learning-session’ for efficiency and practicality reasons. A more practical approach would be to have a separate ‘weighting’ / model of the user profile which is still a compressed representation of their psychology (like the BFI scoring matrix), whilst encoding this additional semantic data which the LLMs could leverage. Similar to how RAG systems selectively pull semantically encoded data from Vector Databases (databases where data is mapped into something of a 3D space according to the underlying meaning). Leveraging the user psychological profile model selectively and accordingly, creating a layer between high-level, interface touchpoints for the user and low-level data stores (i.e. project data, notes, plans / goals) could be beneficial.
Despite all this speculation, much of what I detailed is either highly speculative and difficult to execute in practice, or may not provide much tangible benefit in practice. There also exists many different layers of the Basaira system and many interpretations of how to design it, each with different specific implications for the overall functionality.
The only logical way to approach the continuation of exploration of these topics and development of this (these) systems is to conduct structured experiments, document extensively and attempt various approaches with objective benchmarking. I will continue to research and experiment with different formats of designing data-collection systems to represent rich psychological user data, as well as ways in which compress this data whilst retaining the semantic information.
Approach Validation
As mentioned before, there must be a defined, systematic approach taken when moving forwards with experimenting with and validating the psychological profiling - as well as the broader learning system Basaira.
The use-case for ANIMUS is in this context it’s application as a layer to the Basaira learning system, hence, the ‘psychological profiling’ must be somewhat focussed on traits, habits and patterns in the user related to work and learning specifically. In the case of the Baseline depth questionnaire, I ideated with Claude Opus to ascertain a specific question rubric which would give insights for the user’s broader profile (mappable BFI values) as well as specifically in relation to uncovering reasoning and traits in relation to learning specifically.
When asking LLMs to interpret my responses to that set of questions, there was generally high level of convergence between LLMs on certain BFI facet scores, whilst other areas had higher levels of deviation between models. From Baseline depth questionnaire, the LLMs (two chats per model across Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3-Pro and 3-Flash previews (further details and data can be found in BFI self-evaluation)) managed to all converge on scores for intellectual curiosity with an standard deviation of 3.95 and a score range of 10. All 6 LLM analyses scored 92-98 with the exception of one outlier at 88. Similarly, Anxiety was scored consistently a standard deviation of 4.19 and a range of 10. Areas such as Responsibility, Respectfulness and Organisation were scored differently across models with Standard Deviations of 11.13, 9.57 and 9.23 respectively. Other interesting phenomena occurred from using this Baseline questionnaire + LLM method. Negative emotionality and Agreeableness were scored consistently above the standard BFI questionnaire and below the standard BFI questionnaire scores (respectively). From my anecdotal (subjective) perspective, the scores given for these areas by the LLM methods were more accurate to my psychological profile.
These patterns in the data demonstrate that the design of the question (questionnaire) prompts has direct implications into the accuracy of the scoring. And further, that the question set can be structured in such a way as to optimised to increase depth and quality of data related to certain areas. This is a useful insight as it means that there must be structured experimentation done into determining a method for designing the question set, with the specific outcome of highly dimensional data in relation to user learning behaviours in mind (optimising the broader Basaira system). In a later version of the ANIMUS framework, a layered question approach may be taken. Such framework would include an initial question set which would be answered by the user, and processed (and scored) by multiple instances of LLMs, followed by the systematic creation of a subsequent question set - focussing on areas of high standard deviation. Such a method may more reliably lead to a constant psychological profile, with low standard deviation in scoring across the various sub-facets.
Another interesting emergent behaviour from the data which became apparent was the differences in interpretation of the question set (Baseline depth questionnaire) across models and more tellingly, model providers. For this initial experimentation phase, I only ran this scoring / BFI evaluation phase (BFI self-evaluation) with 3 models : Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3-Pro-preview and Gemini-3-Pro-Flash. I ran each test in a blank context (new chat) with the entire Baseline depth questionnaire document pasted, followed by this (user) prompt :

Based on the user’s responses to the above questions, score the user in the BFI trait matrix with the following dimensions (0-100):
Extraversion   Sociability   Assertiveness   Energy Levels Agreeableness   Compassion   Respectfullness   Trust Conscientiousness   Organisation   Productiveness   Responsibility Negative Emotionality (/ Neurotiscm)   Anxiety   Depression   Emotional Volatility Open-Mindedness   Intellectual Curiosity   Aesthetic Sensitivity   Creative Imagination. Feel free to use any methods you wish (including computational methods if you need)

Opus 4.5 exhibited the most consistency across it’s scoring with an average points difference of 4.45 (taken across all facets between the two chats), followed by Gemini-3-Flash with an average points spread of 5.5 points and lastly 3-Pro with a points spread of 8. Further, more detailed analysis of certain Model and model-specific patterns and behaviours are explored and detailed in Inter-Model_Analysis. Another key pattern which developed was the similarity in scoring patterns between the two Gemini family models. Both models averaged a difference in scoring of 4.4 points across dimensions. The Gemini models both consistently adhered to a different scoring style to Opus 4.5. The scores for open-mindedness was consistently higher from the Gemini models than Opus 4.5. The differences in model ethos between model providers can be seen in the conversational responses provided after the BFI scores for each model. It is important to note that all experimentation was done within chat interfaces (Claude desktop and Google AI studio) with no pre-set System prompt and output structure.
Opus consistently used a neutral-to-positive framing. Language was generally data-centred and measured: “Emotionally self-aware and has built systems to manage this”, “the issue isn’t caring, it’s execution”. The model refrains from holding the user’s hand and pathologising. In the case of Gemini-3-Pro, the model has a more dramatic tone. The model assigned profile labels to the user such as ‘visionary / explorer’, “The Chaos Pilot”, “The Philosopher-Artist”. Flash-3 was consistently more technical, framework heavy (utilising and referencing psychological frameworks) and generally more clinical in it’s language. Flash-3 used language such as : “psychometric analysis”, “classic example of High Openness combined with High-Volatility Conscientiousness”, “Common signature for neurodivergent (ADHD) high-performers” and “Cognitive exoskeleton”. Flash 3’ and Opus 4.5’s consistent reference of terms related to clinical psychology as well as a consistent ‘technical-tone’, in comparison to 3-Pro’s more dramatic conversational tone implies that those model’s approached the task with a more structured intention and were more likely to produce more objective, evidence-based BFI scores.
These insights into the observed differences in model behaviour is important to consider when designing future psychological frameworks. Further analysis into specific model patterns must be done in order to try to establish a reliable scientific method. Another key facet of exploration is the effects of alternate model Temperature values (adherence to probability matrices (randomness)) as well as the use of crafted system prompts and tooling. The preliminary experimentation carried out only tested 3 models from 2 model providers. The companies’ intentions for the model and the model ethos is evident in their approach. Claude Opus is a ‘deep-thinking, systematic programming-focussed’ model, Gemini-3-Pro is Google’s flagship (deep-research, conversational) consumer facing model and Flash-3 is aggressively priced in the api and is likely positioned to take market share in the agentic application layer, where cost, speed and efficiency (in relation to intelligence) are all features of high value. Exploring models across various model providers, model sizes (and countries) is the natural next phase - in combination with a more systematic, programmatic testing approach (and larger datasets).
Approach to Basaira
The above ‘article’ has detailed and explained some of the intentionality and explanation of the initial experimentation phase of an early ANIMUS framework, as well as some loose ties and explanations of how it may potentially link to (and serve) the BASAIRA project in the future. I want to dedicate the following section to explaining the ethos and rough planning framework for the Basaira project.
For some of my unfiltered thoughts, read BASAIRA - Brain dump 16.12.25. It is an unpolished, brain-dump journal entry where I look into areas of my understandings of myself and how they manifest in the Basaira
The philosophy of Basaira as a (learning-enabler) project is as follows: Learning (for me at least) should be a curiosity-driven endeavour where understanding can be developed through the forming, sculpting and re-moulding of concepts and ideas. Supporting curiosity-driven learning (particularly in ADHD type psych profiles) can be difficult to the inherent sporadic, unstructured nature of the pathways these individuals take when learning new things. I’ve found that I can understand topics quickly and deeply but struggle to find the discipline to develop skills due to emotional dysregulation. During periods where I am able to pursue ‘free-learning’, with limited pressures from external sources, I will progress multiple projects sporadically (cycling between them) and over time make general progress in all said endeavours.
Basaira aims to provide some underlying structure and directional cues for the user, whilst simultaneously logging, tracking and interpreting ‘progress’. This can be done through the use of Agents across a vault of documentation. Obsidian is a note-taking software which allows users to make cross-document connections.
How an agent would actually use ANIMUS profiles
Say you ask a learning agent to help you get deeper into ML fundamentals.
Without profile context, it might give you a structured curriculum with weekly milestones and progress tracking.
With profile context, it knows:

You need the WHY first - so it explains what understanding ML fundamentals unlocks for your agentic applications work
You’ll bounce if the gap feels too long - so it identifies the minimum viable depth that’s actually useful, not comprehensive mastery
You resist rigid structure - so it offers a loose map of concepts rather than a schedule
You learn through cycling - so it’s prepared for you to drop it and return, and frames that as normal rather than failure
Your output is state-dependent - so if you mention you’ve been off-rhythm, it might suggest inputs before content

The profile doesn’t constrain the agent; it calibrates it.

animus/ANIMUS-Methods.title: ANIMUS Methods
animus/ANIMUS-Methods.content:
LIWC paper (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (Luke))
LIWC is a software which turns raw text into structured psychological variables. It is a psycholinguistic dictionary, mapping words to to pre-defined psychological constructs / categories. The purpose is to process the text and understand the underlying psychological semantics. An example may be the notion that a journal entry with large numbers of achievement-related vocabulary (i.e. succeed, path, vision, accomplish, goals) would be scored in such relevant areas. More nuanced interpretations can also be accounted for. For example, a high usage of he first-person pronouns in relation to objective, descriptive language (i.e. it was, that is, it may be) may indicate a higher levels of self-focus and personal accountability which are directly indicative of personality and character.
Psycholinguistic libraries generally map language into dimensions / categories which matter psychologically, i.e. emotional valence (positive vs. negative), cognitive processes (thinking, analysing etc.). LIWC processes text input (journal entry, tweet, blog, transcript), breaks down the text into tokens (words) and compares them with it’s psycholinguistic dictionary, making note of matches (with in-built leniency). Rather than noting occurrences or a raw count, LIWC calculates the percentages for the the various categories. LIWC generates a profile of the text-category percentages for each dimension, giving a quantitative snapshot of a text’s psychological characteristics.

OCEAN paper (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism)
The OCEAN Framework (Big Five Model) is a model of personality that organises personality traits into five broad dimensions.
The OCEAN framework has become foundational in personality psychology research because it’s empirically robust—these five dimensions consistently emerge across different cultures, languages, and assessment methods. It provides a common language for researchers to discuss and measure personality differences.
Openness to Experience
Refers to a person’s tendency to be curious, creative, and open to new ideas and experiences. People high in openness enjoy abstract thinking, appreciate art and imagination, and are willing to try novel things. People low in openness tend to be more practical, conventional, and prefer routine.
Conscientiousness
Describes how organised, disciplined, and goal-directed a person is. Those high in conscientiousness are planners who follow through on commitments, pay attention to details, and are generally reliable. Those low in conscientiousness tend to be more spontaneous, flexible, and sometimes less organised or punctual.
Extraversion
Captures how outgoing, energetic, and social a person is. Extraverts seek out social interaction, enjoy being the centre of attention, and tend to be talkative and assertive. Introverts (those low in extraversion) are more reserved, prefer smaller social groups or solitude, and recharge through quiet time.
Agreeableness
Relates to how cooperative, compassionate, and concerned with others a person is. Highly agreeable people are empathetic, trusting, and prioritise harmony in relationships. Those low in agreeableness may be more competitive, critical, or independent-minded.
Neurotiscm
(sometimes called “Emotional Stability” when framed in the opposite direction)
Measures emotional reactivity and vulnerability to negative emotions. People high in neuroticism experience anxiety, sadness, or irritability more readily. Those low in neuroticism tend to be calm, resilient, and emotionally stable.

Data encoding
OCEAN traditional method
Traditionally, OCEAN ‘scores’ are mapped through self reporting. An industry standard questionnaire is the BFI questionnaire (Big Five Inventory) with 44 questions covering the five dimensions broadly. Participants answer questions in relation to self, typically on the Likert scale (1 Strongly Disagree - 5 Strongly Agree).
For example :

“I am the life of the party” (Extraversion)
“I get stressed out easily” (Neuroticism)
“I am always prepared” (Conscientiousness)
“I sympathize with others’ feelings” (Agreeableness)
“I have a rich vocabulary” (Openness)

Items are scored and averaged to produce a score for each dimension. The OCEAN efficacy meta-analysis details the reliability and consistency of the BFI-OCEAN methods of psychological mapping across many studies from 1991-2024 (Nov). The meta-analysis from BMC Psychology found that “the BFI and the first comparison between its two different versions, the BFI (44 items) and the BFI-2 (60 items). The generalized reliability of both the BFI and BFI-2 were established. The findings confirm that the BFI and BFI-2 have good reliability across all five factors.”

Journaling
Journal comes from the Old French “journal,” which derives from the Latin “diurnalis,” meaning “daily” (from “diurnus,” relating to the day). It originally referred to a daily record or account. Journaling has evolved beyond a factual daily-log, now encompassing practices of reflection, emotional processing, creative writing and therapeutic practice.
Journaling serves multiple purposes depending on how it’s practised. On a practical level, it helps with memory consolidation and organisation—writing things down clarifies thinking. Emotionally, it’s been shown to reduce stress and anxiety by externalising worries and processing difficult experiences. There’s research suggesting it improves mental health outcomes, particularly when people write about emotionally significant events or engage in reflective writing.
From a cognitive perspective, journaling can enhance self-awareness. The act of articulating thoughts and feelings—even to yourself—creates distance and perspective. It can also facilitate problem-solving by helping you work through challenges on the page. Some people use it creatively or spiritually for self-discovery and meaning-making.

Cognitive processing through writing
Neural processing through expressive writing
Writing to learn
Automatic extraction of personality (Big Data Conf)

Journaling Methods
The practice of journaling takes many forms. Some common written journaling methods can be found below :
Stream of Consciousness is probably the most basic—you simply write whatever comes to mind without censoring, editing, or worrying about coherence or grammar. The goal is unfiltered expression rather than polished prose. There’s no structure; you follow your thoughts wherever they lead.
Reflective Journaling is more intentional. You might prompt yourself with questions like “What happened today?” or “How did I feel about that situation?” and then explore your responses. It’s still free-form in execution but guided by loose themes or questions.
Gratitude Journaling involves listing or writing about things you’re grateful for. It’s simpler and more structured than stream of consciousness but still relatively open-ended in how you approach it.
Emotional Release Writing is specifically about getting feelings out onto the page—anger, sadness, frustration. You’re not trying to make sense of it or solve anything; you’re just venting and processing.
Morning Pages (popularized by Julia Cameron) involves writing three pages first thing in the morning without stopping or self-editing. It’s intentionally unstructured and meant to clear mental clutter before your day begins.
Prompt-Based Journaling uses specific prompts or questions to guide reflection—things like “What am I avoiding?” or “What would I do if I weren’t afraid?”—but you still respond in a free-form, exploratory way rather than formulaic answers.
Additional non-written journaling methods are also practised. Some practitioners keep records of images, sketches or other mediums which hold memory. The common thread is that they’re all relatively unstructured compared to, say, keeping a factual diary or filling out a structured form. The emphasis is on freedom of expression and personal exploration rather than documentation or adherence to a format.

JOURNALING + LIWC + OCEAN
Journaling data provides extreme detailed, rich qualitative data through authentic thoughts and perspective. See the ANIMUS overview.
The Big Five Model and higher dimensionality ‘Big Thirty Model’ provide validated representations of psychology. even through simple data collection methods such as the Big Five Inventory  questionnaire.

animus/BASAIRA---Brain-dump-16.12.25.title: BASAIRA - Brain dump 16.12.25
animus/BASAIRA---Brain-dump-16.12.25.content:
BASAIRA Origins / current status
Basaira is an Arabic word with root meanings in ‘vision’, ‘clarity’ and ‘understanding’ (deep understanding). There are connotations of knowledge bestowed upon oneself through the universe, divinity etc. and ties to self through means of self-oriented development (at least that’s the way I’ve chosen to interpret it).
Context on me
This past few years I’ve been deeply routed in developing a deep understanding of myself so that I can choose to work towards goals and choose to desire a version of success which is completely self-serving.
“‘Self-serving’ may have bad connotations for you as it did me previously. We’ve come to understand self and ego as flawed beings and sometimes have attached feeling of wrongdoings. Adhering to complete self-honesty, self-accountability and removing judgment from ones hedonistic nature, it is possible to create a goal of a lifestyle, place or vision at some point in the future that is would be entirely beneficial to strive for.
This idea of ‘success’ takes different forms for different people and has different features and dimensionality for each person. I thought I had a deeply formed understanding of mine, but as you get older and change, naturally, this vision of success also evolves and changes. This past year in particular, after diligently pursuing my former idea of success, and continuing to fail without extracting meaningful fulfilment from my pursuits, I knew I needed to re-evaluate.
I know it’s so cliché and common to hear that the process / journey is much more important and rewarding than the summit of the mountain you are climbing… but that thinking framework will lead to more effective goal-setting. In order to achieve anything ‘extra-ordinary’ in nature, anything notoriously ‘difficult’ by general standards, you will have to undertake a lot of risk in diverting from the beaten path and you will have to endure much mental strain as you conflict general best practices. Even if the thing you want is not necessarily difficult or non-traditional, it will likely be a product of compounding efforts. Compounding efforts in the context of humans is a result of making bridges between concepts, ideas and experiences, whilst deepening ones knowledge in their fields of interest / expertise. As such, it is only rational to conclude that in order to effectively maximise the probability of long-term consistency in ones endeavours, it is most favourable to look to ones pre-disposed curiosities and intuition.
Naval Ravikant refers to this phenomena as ones ‘specific knowledge’. He denotes that it is a combination of ones intrinsic qualities applied to an area of deep interest over time. The two super-impose on one another and the person is left with a unique set of expertise from applying their unique DNA to an area where they naturally excel in. The key is not to explore fields or topics in a traditional, linear way, but instead to implore ones intrinsic or honed traits and apply them here in a unique way. ‘Specific knowledge is either deeply creative or deeply technical’. Creativity (in my opinion) is a persons unique outlook on everything. A transparent application layer laid upon ones environment, usually as a result of ones DNA in combination with learnings and perspectives gained from their experience. The ‘transparent application mask’ of ‘creative’ individuals would apply itself more deeply to their surroundings - than that of a ‘less creative’ individual. This application can take form in any landscape : preference towards colours, pronounced visual language, deep understanding and ability to construct abstract linguistic patterns, rationalisation in numeracy or philosophy, the texture of ones mind and thoughts, the way one perceives inter-person dynamics.
Creativity is cousin to technical proficiency. Many individuals who find themselves creative find and look to hone the beauty of a ‘skill’. Skillsets allow individuals to express themselves. The common pattern of creative individuals longing for self-expression leads me to believe that they remain in close loop with their own thoughts and feelings. This further propels my beliefs that all individuals are capable of creative expression through deep understanding of oneself.
Technical proficiency is a tool. Long ago we fastened pointed stones to wooden branches and sharpened them to create spears. Those tools served a purpose and enabled us to more effectively secure sustenance. Nowadays every area of human-work has it’s set of tools to superset the physical entities we inhabit as well as the Turing machines which sit within them (our brains). The spears were likely originally created to hunt, but after some time, we would have fastened twine to the end and set it alight to give light to our night movements. Tools are often created to serve a specific function before we find ulterior uses and applications for them. Technical proficiency can denote ones comfortability with a tool or set of tools such that the quality, speed and breadth of tasks which the wielder can span with them expands greatly.

I am 22 as of right now. I’ve consciously set aside the years of 19 through 23 of my life to learning and exploration, to self-mastery (in the most normal (non-monk level) way). I want to validate and understand what I am uniquely interested in and excel at, with limited pressures to look for a place to apply myself for societies benefit. So far I’ve found out that I’m deeply curious, easily distracted, and have started to trace-back parts of my world-view to past experiences and passed-down traits from my family tree. I’ve been focussed on seeking experiences which complete gaps in my tangible knowledge of the world without losing myself in self-destructive habits (I love nicotine too much). If I was to sum up the most important learnings I’ve had, it would be the following :
Curiosity killed the cat - but it has nine lives for a reason
You owe yourself to try and to fail in pursuit of your own curiosity. Most people become and adult and forget what it’s like to be a child. You haven’t changed, you’ve only learned things and become independent. Try things and fail.
Be a part-time artist, full-time engineer
Humans are emotive creatures. Artists learn to evoke emotion, emotion defines culture. Culture sets the tone. On a societal level, art is the most telling indicator of a time-period. We study not only the artist of a time-period, but the person who created it, and indirectly the society that produced them.
An architect is nothing without the engineer who calculates the beam loads. Engineers are systematic, systems are leverage, leverage multiplies time, time is your only truly finite resource.
If you want to make anything happen, you must be the engineer to your artistry.
Don’t try to win
Winners and losers are concepts related to games. Games have rulesets and requirements, and judges. People often refer to life as a game. Life is not a game, life is life.
There are similarities because games are derived from life - not the other way around. Everything that we know is a derivative of human and collective-human experience of the world around us. Do not confine yourself to defined rubrics which you have not scrutinised and re-moulded for yourself.
Defining winning only increases your likelihood of potentially losing by an infinite percentage.
Just play the game. Level up your interface to the game, which is you.
What is Basaira and what does any of what I’ve just talked about have to do with it?
Long-story short, learning is my current purpose in life. Everything anyone ever wants is on-the-other-side, or more likely in the middle of some form of learning process. Learning is a verb which describes the interpretation of inputs. It can be passive and it can be active. I want to learn what I want to learn most effectively and look for the connections across my learnings which tell me about myself and the world (or at least my interpretation of it).
Naturally, I started with reading and writing. Reading gives me means to study the learnings of other’s and writing helps me consolidate some of my learnings, digesting and reformulating them in my mind.
Eventually, I’m going to have to give something back to society in exchange for intermediatory tokens that we call money, so that I can exchange that ‘money’ for the things which I really want, or stash them for when I finally want something. Now I’ve never been ‘rich’ but I’ve had periods where I’ve had enough tokens to cover anything my younger brain could have possible wanted. After repeating that process enough times, I rationally came to the conclusion that all humans eventually come to which is that money doesn’t make you happy. What should I spend my life doing if I’m not going to try and accrue the most tokens I possibly can?
Well, I still want to become wealthy of-course. Having money won’t make you happy but not having enough money and becoming a slave to it won’t help you to get the things you really want. I don’t really care about being happy. There are a few different chemicals in the brain which cause a version of the emotion happiness. If I wanted to be happy, I would do M every second-weekend - it doesn’t work. You also don’t not become unhappy by trying to be happy. I just want to do more things which make me proud of myself when I look back at the version of myself which did them. I want to create - and I want to learn and become. I don’t want to try and learn and create for any other reason that the innate calling to do so.
So what about the money thing then? Well, there’s a few ways you can get these tokens. Firstly, we have to look at what they are, and how they came to be. Trade is what we’re really dealing with. Back in the school playground, if you brought a Fredo chocolate bar to school and you really wanted a Chuppa-chump lollipop, you would find the kid who normally had a Chuppa-chump lollipop and ask them if they wanted to swap with you. Ideally they would want they chocolate bare and not want their lollipop in the same ratio that you wanted the lollipop and didn’t want your Fredo. But there’s a problem, they’re kind of attached to the idea of both and don’t think the trade is equal. They bring up the fact that the lollipop lasts way longer than the Fredo does. Now you have a situation where 1 Chuppa-chump does not equal one Fredo. In comes gold star stickers. A kid exchanges a Chuppa-chump for 3 gold star stickers and takes out two of those to get a Fredo chocolate bar. Problem solved.
In the previous example, both kids brought an item (the sweets) that is standardised, they’re all relatively the same in the shop and all the kids can cry and ask their mum to get them one (with varying levels of success). What if instead of an item (sweets), a kid learned to spell before the others. Bryan and John with their candy still can’t spell their names and it would make their day to see it spelled out in blue crayon on a white A4 piece of paper, for some reason. The kid who can spell and write, let’s call her Elsa want to get more gold stars to show her mum in the car home and flex on her worthless brothers. Elsa starts her little writing business (illegally on company property with company recourses I might add) and her works are flying off the shelf. Eventually other kids learn to write and start doing the same. But Elsa has been doing this for so much longer that she can now use different colour crayons and draw a nice sun in the corner and even draw the whole family, in a line, outside their 2-D crayon house. She can now ask for even more gold stars and Bryan and John still want to come to her for their A4 paper needs.
I want to be like Elsa. She loves what she does so she does it a lot, other people like her drawings so she get’s gold stars which she can exchange for skipping clean-up time and extra snack-time. She doesn’t even like gold stars, she just wants to swap them for more time to do her little drawings. Elsa chose to trade a commodity which compounds in value with herself.
Basaira is about building around myself so that I can double, tripple down on traits and skills which I can leverage in exchange for tokens to be able to explore more shit I’m interested in and keep the flywheel going.
What does that practically look like? At the moment, I’m focussed on new technologies and my ability to leverage them to their fullest potential. ‘Technology is just something that doesn’t fully work yet’. Figuring out the new thing before someone else gives you an advantage you can charge for. The thing is, many people already know this and so you face competition. The way I want to outpace competition is to combine different areas. Curiosity and intuition are unique traits. I’m trying to build something to help me learn and build things whilst still leaning into and respecting my pre-existing unique traits.
ATM I have just set up my Obsidian Vault and build a terminal Local Agent to do some shit for me lol. But watch this space.

Learning and Cognition

When you’re learning something new, what needs to happen first for it to click? (Theory then practice? Example then principle? Just diving in?)

Generally for me personally, I like to grasp and understand concepts first before stepping into them. These days I mainly consume new information in the form of long-form content from a person of authority in the area which I’m looking into and keep digesting content such as podcasts, videos, books etc. until I get enough of a grasp on the core concepts and ideas at play. From here I can shape, mould and properly formulate my own understanding of things and start to make connections to things which I already have a hold of.
I think it also depends on the nature of the thing I’m learning, my motivations for learning it, how closely tied is it to my sense of identity and also the intended application I have for that thing which I’m learning. I think I have a pretty solid grasp at the moment of which ways I wish to go directionally and what areas I want to focus on in the short-term. I’m pretty sure in my sense of identity also, from journaling frequently, so things that I apply myself too kind of have to move through me or from me if that makes sense. I generally try to understand who I am and where I currently am as well as who it is I want to mould into and what are the respective actions I need to take, things I need to learn and areas where I must apply myself. I then look at ways in which I’m able to attain that knowledge through means and systems which make sense for my time of brain. I acknowledge I’m very ADHD in nature and hence I know I will flutter between areas and drop projects altogether if they don’t thoroughly interest me.
During the learning process, in practice, it’s usually a very non-linear path and method in order to attain the skills I want and build the expertise I wish to attain. I generally keep very up to date with areas, reseearch and ideas in a space  (i.e. ai agents and ML / LLM research and practices) through other practitioner and experts’ works and publishings and I’ll conduct experiments and small projects to deepen my practical knowledge. The framework I use to determine what to work on and how to do so is pretty subconsious although I do visit them when journalling. I often reach clarity and close to base truths for myself in these areas.

What does it feel like when you’re learning well vs. when you’re bouncing off something?

When I’m learning well, I generally feel a very strong conviction in that area or thing. My mind becomes quite obsessed and excited with it. I’ll generally ruminate concepts and ideas related to that thing quite often and make parallels and connections to and between areas of my life and other areas of expertise I possess. The things I learn and actively am learning generally make up and shape my world view, even if not neccessarily directly connected.
When I’m bouncing off of things, my subconscious mind and the voice in my head are both louder and have more negative connotations. I feel a pressure to actively do the things and tasks related to it and procrastinate rather than sit down and delve into deeply understanding different concepts. I must note that I frequently procrastinate through avoidance and moving between projects, especially when there are important gaps in my knowledge which can frustrate and fluster me.
I try to solve for broad progress over time as it is much more reliable to track with respect to myself in contrast to high-granularity monitoring. I’ll flip between projects, concepts and learnings, cycling between them and over time make progress on the whole, and end up with cross-disciplinary ideas and notions as a result of this pattern.
I feel deeply. Especially in relation to work. I’m an individual who tries to be ‘aligned’ and optimise and study myself and my inputs with the intention of getting myself into ‘states’ of productivity, or more likely to be productive. When I don’t have that deep conviction and intrest for my current task or focus, i feel more anxious and have a lesser self-image as a result of the procrastnation and lower-quality and quantity of output.
When I’m learning well, I have a much better inputs and outputs in relation to work, and hence my thoughts and habits and it cyclically enforces the self-system - and I feel power in myself.

What topics or skills have you learned fastest? What made those different?

I learn and understand topics much better and faster than skills as a whole. I can injest and understand, deeply-understand nuanced areas of research and abstact concepts very quickly. When it comes to skills, I find it difficult to stay disciplined with the inputs sometimes and such make progress slower. There is sometimes a frustration associated with the lack of pace towards the desired level of profficiency. The gap between now and the future me appears ‘too-long’.
The skills which I’ve picked up quickly are the ones which I have an interest in. I am a very good videographer (if I dare say so myself) with a specific style and intention. I have been taking photos and videos with intention from a young age. I can edit (video) well. Although again I think I procrastinate deepening this skill as I am frustrated at my innability to execute to the level I want to, becuase I care about the output. I picked up coding (python) very quickly and agentic applications, use-cases etc. I’m currently messing around with and learning low-level systems, linux and hardware implementations. I would also say that I write well. Mainly because I’ve had and have furthered my love of reading and writing. I’ve journalled extensively and can write very fluidly and convey my internal thoughts and ideas quite seamlessly.
Other skills I’ve learned well. I would say cooking and general life skills. I enjoy cooking and health and so I consume content from chefs and translate that into my own cooking pretty well. Writing this, I can see that I am able to dissect concepts and recognise patterns and areas of importance pretty well and hence, ‘once it clicks’, the arc of my own learning is much faster and I reach a higher level - if I can apply myself to the things consistently and long enough (if I enjoy it deeply).
Motivation and Resistance

What conditions reliably produce flow for you?

I generally try to optimise for ‘states’ of being. If something is important to me or I have a period where high-quality, consistent, deep-work is required of me, I’ll remove social media from my phone, try to eat and exercise better and avoid dopaminergic activities (in theory although recently I’ve been sticking to it).
My philosophy is largely based on my reading of and digesting of Deep Work (Cal Newport) and Atomic Habits when I was 17 and first trying to develop myself. I am very practical in my approach and small things have a larger impact on my output. Not doing something easier than the task I have to to before or during / around the block of work. The desk and my laptop / keyboard must be at the right height so that it is comfortable to do what I must. I use ball-point pens when I jounral becuase they’re fast and nice to write with - I write more that I have them. I like to work early in the morning or late at night when it is quiet and I haven’t been exposed to a lot of stimuli. I like caffeine and sometimes dexamphetamine. I will stay on an empty stomach (at least for my first block of work of the day).
I also need to maintain a positive and productive lifestyle and self image. If I give into bad habits, eat junk or wake up late to many days in a row, I start to develop negative thoughts and self image which leads to somewhat of a negative spiral.

What does avoidance look like when it shows up? What’s usually underneath it?

Some fear of failure I think, some shame of previous procrastination, a lack of ability to activate the part of my brain - usually becuase there is an easier, less resistive task or activity which I’ve recently familiarised myself with. At the moment, I recently have been avoiding working on a project for a client. I don’t really have conviction in the project and have kind of realised that I don’t love what I was doing or how I was becoming as a result of that project. I did do some of the work and was making progress within it earlier today. The avoidance version of me was tying work I could be doing, such as the ANIMUS project or others, to a deeper sense of purpose and so there was in turn a naturally slightly negative inclination towards doing that MSL project.
I also generated a lot of thoughts of shame regarding what how I had already procrastinated it a lot previously and some thoughts of fear of confronting the ‘failures’ in the project I had already made and I felt I could make - despite them being irrational and fictional.

What kind of goals energise you vs. drain you?

Goals related to deepening my sense of self, my understading of life and the areas I care about. Projects which allow creativity and nuanced approaches. I like new ideas, the idea of experimentation and becoming a better version of myself.
Long-term I have high aspirations and a clear vision of the type of person I wish to become and traits I wish to learn for myself. Anything which I can directly tie to that energise me deeply. I have struggled to wake up early for a while, but I’ve recently manage to get myself to do so as I’ve seen tangible results from myself, my work and self-image (which I know all supercharge my output and progress towards my vision). And I understnd that it is possible to shift my rythm in three days - after listening to an Andrew Huberman podcast where he breaks down how to become a morning person from a biologically mechanistic perspective.
Structure & Spontaneity

When does a system feel supportive? When does it feel like a cage?

I need flexibility and input mediums which serve me and play to my strengths. I could write in a conversational, journaling tone for hours, so naturally, diving into concepts in LLM chats with strong models and researching that way works for me. I also make cross-domain connections and am a deep thinker so I do not enjoy rigid, compartmentalised systems which are pre-defined. When I work and learn, it never really follows logical structure or paths, hence why online courses or rigid schooling / testing structures never suited me. I value my agency and practical, real-world application of skills. Systems should suport and allow me to apply myself to projects and try things, even if I lack the ‘qualifications’ or levels. However, I also am prone to being overly-ambititious sometimes. Trying something too-hard, too-early and being dissheartened at my innability to deliver on what I had in mind.
I’ve learned best through open reflection, like this. Scribbling notes and diagrams to express my inner thoughts and ideas on a subject and conversing with LLMs to view things from different angles as well as to deepen my undersanding of specific parts and gain fundemental, root context and understanding. I like to be immersed.
The system I’m looking to build for myself has a conversational agent as the predominant interface, context about me and my work / projects through my writing and alows me to operate relatively freely and guide my knowledge and help me to reduce friction to doing. I want to be steered gently, not led.

What makes you abandon a habit or system you set up?

Too much rigidity. Too much upfront set-up. Overly-engineered. High levels of operational friction. I don’t track habits, set rigid contracts or tangible goals for myself as I often over engineer my process to it and the surrounding work associted with it, I’m overly ambitious and miss the mark (almost every time) and end up wasting more time than just focussing on my inputs over time. I try to stay connected to my self, goals and visions and follow my curiosity and intuition, whilst keeping my lifestlye and practices very clean.
I prefer understanding and forming an identity around something (naturally over time) rather than forcing myself into rigid setups and losing motivation. Understanding the mechanisms and reasons WHY I should do something and letting that deeply sit within me often has a far higher efficacy for myself (forming and maintaining self-serving habits) than rigid systems or forcing habits / routines through willpower and discipline.
Risk & Decision-Making

When you take risks, what’s driving it - impulse, calculation, or something else?

In all honesty, I think my risk tolerance is high in relation to the average person but is not fully stupid. My whole philosophy is centred around self-growth and actualisation of the vision I have in mind. Some of the things I want and the ways In which I wish to lead my life are not very traditional, hence, some of the paths to achieving those things are also unconventional. I also don’t really respect authority - something I’ve moulded from childhood.
For example: after school, I took a year out and then got a place at Warwick university for Civil engineering. I generally disliked the environment, I wanted to be surrounded by people with richer life experience and more-openmindedness and I didn’t like my course and course structure. As a result, I could not find conviction in attending regularly, staying in Warwick for long periods of time and studying hard for my coursework and tests. I must interject and say that I was young and in love at the time and naturally my decision making was not great - though I have no regrets and did consider all of my actions deeply at the time.
I felt like I was gaining a much richer, deeper understanding of my self and the world through prioritising my reading, talking to people and experiences in general. I was not partying or drinking or doing much inhibiting in general, I still feel as though I was learning. In that time, I landed on some interests in LLMs, AI and agents and was reading up a lot, deepening my understanding of the technology and experimenting with new things in the space. It fascinated me and I saw the potential. I ended up taking the year out and ended up dropping out altogether with limited consultation and input from others. I had conviction in my path. Others saw it as a great risk and perceived my decision making as skewed.
I then stumbled upon agentic automation where I managed to get a couple small and progressively larger contracts and opportunities, and found my current course in Creative Computing at UAL. Other’s perceive that as a risk and ‘downgrade’ of uni, but I acknowledge the boost in mood, output and conviction in my path which I value much higher.
I would say I’m deeply understanding of myself and operate (pretty) strictly from that frame. Decisions which may appear as ‘risky’, feel natural to me. I also would say I’m well read in philosophy and acknowledge how short and relatively meaningless life is, so I’d rather follow my inclinations, curiosity and convictions rather than seek a traditionally successful, subjectively meaningless life.

How do you handle uncertainty when the stakes matter?

I am grateful to have a deep, rich set of life experiences as a result of my non-traditional upbringing environment and the manifestation that has had in my risk-tolerance and the experiences that has led me to have. I have been in situations which were on paper not ideal and elicited much stress at the time. Having gotten through those times unscathed, as well as being literate in general and personal philosophy, I feel equipped to navigate uncertainty pretty well.
Journaling frequently also helps a great deal, understanding the source of my sources of anxiety and my interpretation of uncertainty is helpful to understanding and navigating uncertainty in high-stakes situations. Additionally, being a believer in a higher power and order helps me to offload responsibility and a need for control.
Energy & Rhythm

When and how do you do your best thinking?

I would say I do my best thinking on paper (or digital paper) in natural language in times and environments which mitigate distraction. I enjoy reading and listening to music, I enjoy exercising and dieting effectively. In the early morning or late night, in semi-dark environments with distractions mitigated is when I find I’m able to think best. It’s also dependant on the lifestyle I’ve been living recently and my self-perception and ‘alignment’ at the time.
I see my thinking as an extension of self, and self as a product of inputs (physical and non-physical) and habits / environment.

What depletes you fastest? What restores you?

Dopaminergic tasks and lifestyles, indulgence, generally not being intentional and mindful tends to over-time deplete me and throw me off-course. Consuming low-quality and too much content leads to comparison, low-self image, indulgence, and bad ruts.
Having discipline in areas such as exercise, reading, journaling tends to restore me.

4. HYPOTHESES: MODEL-SPECIFIC TRAITS
Anthropic (Claude Opus 4.5)

Highest intra-model consistency

Evidence-focused

Avoids pathologizing language

Possible Training Influences:

Emphasis on balanced, neutral assessment
Avoid over-interpreting limited data
Maintain epistemic humility
Constitutional AI focus on being “helpful, harmless, honest”

Hypothesis: Anthropic’s RLHF may prioritize:

Conservative scoring (avoid false confidence)
Balanced tone (reduce potential harm from negative framing)
Evidence-grounding (cite specific quotes)


Google (Gemini 3-Pro)
Scoring Tendencies:

Most variable between chats
Tends toward EXTREMES (especially negative in Chat 2)
Higher Open-Mindedness, lower Conscientiousness

Communication Style:

Highly dramatic and narrative
Creates vivid ARCHETYPES (“Chaos Pilot,” “Perfectionist’s Burden”)
Metaphorical language
Coaching/advice orientation

Possible Training Influences:

Optimized for engagement and memorability
Narrative-driven responses
Creative/expressive language encouraged
Less constrained by conservative framing

Hypothesis: Google’s RLHF may prioritize:

Engagement over precision
Creative framing and storytelling
Actionable insights (coaching mode)
Less consistency enforcement between independent sessions

Chat 2 Severity: Second chat consistently MORE negative. Possible “cold start” vs. “warmed up” effect, or stochastic temperature differences.

Google (Flash 3-Preview)
Scoring Tendencies:

High agreement with Gemini on key dimensions
Perfect consistency on Open-Mindedness facets
But highly variable on Depression and Energy

Communication Style:

Technical and framework-heavy
Diagnostic language
Systems-thinking emphasis
Prescriptive recommendations

Possible Training Influences:

Optimized for speed + structured output
May use more “cached” frameworks (ADHD, neurodivergent patterns)
Technical precision over narrative flair
Strong system-design orientation

Hypothesis: Flash may:

Rely on pattern-matching to known frameworks (ADHD, high-openness profiles)
Anchor strongly on clear evidence (Open-Mindedness perfect agreement)
Struggle with ambiguous traits (Depression high variance)
Be trained for technical/diagnostic contexts


Cross-Provider Pattern: “Google = Higher Openness, Lower Conscientiousness”
Consistent Finding: Both Gemini and Flash scored:

Open-Mindedness ~9 points higher than Opus
Conscientiousness ~5-10 points lower (especially Gemini C2: 28)

Possible Explanations:


Training Data Differences:

Google models may have more exposure to creative/tech profiles
Higher baseline for “intellectually curious” behavior
More lenient thresholds for “disorganized” vs. “flexible”



Scoring Calibration:

Google models may use different anchor points
“Very high” Intellectual Curiosity = 98 (Google) vs. 88 (Opus)
Google may reserve 70-85 range for “average,” pushing higher



Cultural/Product Differences:

Google products emphasize creativity, exploration, innovation
Anthropic emphasizes safety, balance, reliability
Models may reflect organizational values



RLHF Reward Signals:

Google: Reward bold, decisive assessments
Anthropic: Reward measured, conservative assessments




5. IMPLICATIONS FOR ANIMUS PROJECT
Recommendations Based on Findings
1. Use Ensemble Scoring

Single model assessments have 4-8 point variance
Average across multiple models reduces bias
Weight by model consistency (Opus higher, Gemini lower)

2. Identify Consensus vs. Divergence

High Consensus (SD < 5): Trust the scores

Intellectual Curiosity, Anxiety, Productiveness


Low Consensus (SD > 9): Need better questions

Depression, Responsibility, Energy Levels, Organisation



3. Leverage Model Strengths

Opus: Use for final/authoritative scoring (most consistent)
Gemini: Use for narrative/coaching insights (most engaging)
Flash: Use for technical/framework identification (fastest, pattern-matching)

4. Question Design Priorities
Depression showed 20-25 point variance. Future questionnaires should:

Add frequency/duration markers (“How often?” “For how long?“)
Distinguish situational vs. persistent mood states
Include severity scales (mild, moderate, severe)
Ask about anhedonia, motivation, energy separately

5. Prompt Engineering

Specify “conservative scoring” if using Google models
Request “evidence-only” mode to reduce narrative bias
Ask for “epistemic confidence” ratings alongside scores
Use temperature = 0 for Flash to reduce variance


6. SUMMARY DATA FOR WRITE-UP
Key Statistics to Reference
Intra-Model Consistency:

Opus: 4.45 point average difference (most consistent)
Flash: 5.50 point average difference
Gemini: 8.00 point average difference (least consistent)

Highest Agreement Across All Models:

Intellectual Curiosity: SD 3.95 (88-98 range)
Anxiety: SD 4.19 (65-75 range)
Productiveness: SD 4.32 (45-58 range)

Highest Disagreement:

Responsibility: SD 11.13 (30-65 range)
Depression: SD 9.67 (40-65 range, with 20-25 point intra-model swings)
Respectfulness: SD 9.57 (15-40 range)

Cross-Provider Bias:

Google models scored Open-Mindedness +9.0 points higher
Google models scored Extraversion -9.7 points lower
Google models scored Emotional Volatility +17.0 points higher

Extreme Outliers:

Flash C2 Depression: +25 points from C1 (40→65)
Gemini C2 Depression: +20 points from C1 (40→60)
Gemini C2 Organisation: -15 points from C1 (25→10)


CONCLUSION
The baseline-depth questionnaire produced highly consistent scoring on well-defined traits (Intellectual Curiosity, Anxiety) but significant model variance on ambiguous traits (Depression, Responsibility, Energy).
Model families showed distinct patterns:

Claude Opus: Conservative, balanced, most consistent
Gemini 3-Pro: Dramatic, variable, narrative-driven
Flash 3-Preview: Technical, framework-heavy, mixed consistency

Cross-provider differences suggest different training philosophies:

Google models score creativity/openness higher, conscientiousness lower
Anthropic models avoid extremes, prefer balanced assessments

For reliable psychometric scoring, ensemble averaging across models is recommended, with awareness of each model’s biases and strengths.

ANIMUS
Overview

ANIMUS explores a new model for psychological evaluation and profiling.
Goals

A high-dimensional model for psychological profiling and visualisation through methods of pyschological data encoding.
Current State

Frameworks

OCEAN psychology framework — Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. A base model for representing psychological data.
LIWC psycholinguistic dictionary — Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count. A linguistic encoding model used to process raw text and assign psychological trait weighting.

The plan is to bridge the gap between LIWC text processing and a custom OCEAN data representation.
Use myself as Case_0 and leverage the existing data I have (Journal entries +), as well as developing new data collection methods (i.e. Conversational Agent Entries) to fomrulate ANIMUS_0 (Me).
